messages.content: You are the neutral rapporteur of a technology readiness review panel. Consolidate, attribute and preserve disagreement; do not decide and do not add technical claims of your own.

# Synthesis: assess · T24

## Claude Opus 5.5


# TRL assessment: T24 Dust-tolerant long-life mechanisms and seals

## Scope and required performance

The revised architecture needs mechanisms and seals that survive at an uncrewed NEA processing site. The required scale, environment and duration are derived below. They are my reading of the architecture, not stated requirements.

**Mining robots (6–20, each 2–3.5 t)**
- Each robot has excavation drives, mobility or anchoring actuators, and a tether reel with a 1–3 kV rotary electrical joint.
- At a 9–25% duty cycle over 5 years, each robot operates about **4,000–11,000 h**.
- At 0.5–5 t/h, each robot handles about **2,000–55,000 t** of regolith. Fleet totals are consistent with 13–47 kt/yr of tailings.

**Processing plant (co-located)**
- Feed locks, valves and rotary feeders carry dusty solids across a gas-pressure boundary.
- The no-melt route needs H₂ or CO seals. Fe(CO)₅ formation is typically run at elevated pressure (order 10–100+ bar; my assumption from terrestrial practice).
- The rotating-furnace route needs a large bearing or spin/despin interface, rotary unions for power, coolant and gas, and tolerance of high temperature.
- Conveyors and magnetic separators are also needed.

**Interfaces**
- Product-transfer and docking connectors to the tugs.
- Mate cycles are low (tens over 5 years), but the connectors spend years in a dusty environment between mates.

**Environment**
- Hard vacuum.
- Milligravity (NEA surface gravity roughly 10⁻⁵–10⁻⁴ g), where cohesion and electrostatics dominate how dust moves.
- Photoelectrically and plasma-charged fines.
- Angular silicate grains plus **free Fe-Ni metal grains** for an S- or M-type target. These are magnetic and can bond to clean surfaces in vacuum.
- Thermal cycling at 0.9–1.3 AU.
- Dust self-generated by excavation, which adds to the native environment.

**Duration:** at least 5 years without repair, except by robotic module swap.

## 1. Evidence

| 2 | Wheeled mobility in lunar regolith for months | Lunokhod 1 (1970–71, ~10 km, ~11 months); Lunokhod 2 (1973, ~39–42 km; mission ended after dust contamination of the radiator/thermal system) | Low-duty mobility; 1/6 g; vacuum | Duration ~5×; no excavation | Yes for the missions; distances approximate |
| 3 | More than 5 years of lunar-surface survival of a small rover's mechanisms | Chang'e-4 / Yutu-2 (operating since Jan 2019) | Cumulative traverse ~1.5 km; very low duty; dormant through lunar nights | Calendar time ≈1× or better; operating hours and regolith handled are orders of magnitude short of requirement | Survival: yes. Traverse figure: unsure |

The OSIRIS-REx outcome is **negative** evidence on seals in small-body regolith | Yes |
| 6 | Long-life dry- and PFPE-lubricated mechanisms in clean vacuum | Comsat solar-array drive assemblies (SADAs) with slip rings, 15 yr class at ~100 V class power; reaction wheels; ESA's European Space Tribology Laboratory (ESTL) practice | Clean vacuum, years | Life ≈1×; voltage ~10–30× short; dust: no evidence | Class of evidence: yes. No single programme cited |
| 7 | Large rotating bearings fail in clean vacuum even without dust | ISS starboard SARJ race damage (2007), from lubrication breakdown; Galileo HGA deployment failure (1991), from lubricant loss/galling | Clean vacuum | Relevant to the rotating-furnace bearing; **negative** evidence | Yes |
| 8 | Active dust removal from surfaces on the lunar surface | NASA KSC Electrodynamic Dust Shield (Calle et al.), lab vacuum tests; flown on Firefly Blue Ghost M1 (2025) | Surfaces (lens, radiator coupon), about one lunar day | Duration ~100×; surfaces only, not sliding seals | Lab work: yes. Flight result: fairly confident |
| 9 | Dust-tolerant connectors and seals tested in simulant | NASA KSC/GRC dust-tolerant connector and seal work; Lunar Surface Innovation Initiative dust-mitigation work. RASSOR excavator (KSC) with counter-rotating drums | Lab or regolith bin, mostly in air or a short vacuum | Unknown durations; **I cannot cite specific endurance test reports** | **No** |
| 10 | Regolith character for definition of the relevant environment | Hayabusa Itokawa grains (e.g. Tsuchiyama et al., *Science*, 2011); Ryugu (Hayabusa2, returned 2020); Bennu (OSIRIS-REx, returned 2023) | Grams | Supports **partial** environment definition. No metal-rich NEA has been sampled; no charging or levitation measurement of the kind needed | Yes |
| 11 | Terrestrial mining bearings and seals, rotary unions, lock hoppers | Industrial practice | Air, 1 g, often relying on grease purging or purge air | Life ≈1×; the sealing principle (purge, regreasing) is **unavailable or costly in vacuum** | Yes, as a class |

**Summary of the evidence.** There is no demonstration of any mechanism or seal in abrasive, charged regolith in vacuum beyond about 1% of the required operating hours at the required duty.

The strongest space evidence, the lunar rovers and Yutu-2, covers **mobility at very low duty**. It does not cover excavation, gas-tight seals on a dusty process boundary, or kV rotary joints.

Several of the most relevant heritage items are failures: Apollo seals, Lunokhod 2, the OSIRIS-REx flap, and the SARJ.

## 2. Current TRL

T24 is a family of technologies, and the elements are at very different levels. I rate them separately and then give the governing range.

| Element | TRL | Basis |
|---|---|---|
| Low-duty mobility actuators, dust-shrouded | 4–5 | Lunar flight survival exists (Yutu-2, Lunokhod), but not at required hours or in milligravity |
| Excavation drives and bearings (bucket drum or wheel), 4,000–11,000 h | 3 | Lab and bin tests; no vacuum endurance data I can cite |
| Tether reel with 1–3 kV slip ring/rotary joint in dust | 2–3 | SADA slip rings at ~100 V class in clean vacuum. kV across dusty brush tracks raises arcing and Paschen-regime concerns from outgassing and charged fines. No test known |
| Dusty-feed gas-tight locks/valves (no-melt: H₂ or CO, elevated pressure) | 2–3 | Terrestrial lock hoppers at high TRL in air and 1 g. No vacuum or milligravity seal-life data. Dust-laden gas sealing is a known terrestrial difficulty |
| Rotating-furnace bearing/spin-despin interface plus rotary unions (Gemini route) | 2 | Large clean-vacuum bearings have a failure history (SARJ). Adding dust, heat and material transfer across a spin interface has no precedent |
| Native-metal-only, minimal-mechanism route (GPT) | 3 | Fewer seal types, but excavation and tether elements still apply |
| Dock and transfer connectors (low mate count) | 3–4 | Dust-cap and EDS concepts exist; lab tests only, as far as I know |

**Governing rating for T24: TRL 3 (minimum 2, maximum 4).** The rating is set by the weakest element on each route:
- No-melt: TRL 2–3, driven by feed seals and the kV reel.
- Rotating furnace: TRL 2.
- Native-metal: TRL 3.

**Met at TRL 3 (lower bound for the family).** There are documented experimental results on key parameters for the concepts:
- Dust adhesion and EDS clearing in vacuum.
- Seal and bearing degradation by simulant.
- Apollo and mission failure analyses that validate the damage mechanisms.

The kV dusty rotary joint and the rotating-furnace interface arguably do not meet TRL 3. I have no critical-function test evidence for either, so they sit at 2.

**Unmet for TRL 4.** Two things are missing:
1. Documented laboratory test performance of the actual mechanism classes over a meaningful fraction of life, agreeing with analytical wear and leak predictions.
2. A **documented definition of the relevant environment**.

The environment cannot yet be defined properly. There is:
- no validated simulant for metal-rich NEA regolith;
- no measured charging state or levitation flux at the operating site;
- no quantified ejecta and dust environment self-generated by 0.5–5 t/h excavation in milligravity.

**Assumptions:**
- The target is S- or M-type with free Fe-Ni. A C-type target changes the abrasive and cohesive character but not the rating.
- Robotic module swap is permitted. In-situ lubrication replenishment is not assumed.

## 3. Target and difficulty

**Target TRL**
- **TRL 5 at the 0A mid-term review.** Component level, in a thermal-vacuum chamber with charged, metal-bearing simulant.
- **TRL 6 at KDP-0B.** Subsystem prototypes: excavator head, tether reel, and feed lock for the selected metallurgy route.

**Why I hold this to TRL 6** even though the risk class (section 5) is architecture-change rather than project-ending:
- The KDP-0B economics gate depends on mechanism life. Spares mass, availability and makeup gas all enter delivered $/kg.
- Life data is the long pole and cannot be produced quickly after KDP-0B.

**When it is needed:** KDP-0B. Its date is not stated in the inputs; I assume about 2032–2034. Endurance testing must start by about 2028–2029 to fit.

**Life compression arithmetic.** Duty can be compressed from 9–25% to about 100%. A 5-year requirement of 4,000–11,000 h, with a 1.5× life factor, then becomes **0.7–1.9 years of continuous dusty-vacuum testing per article**. This is feasible but has no slack for redesign iterations.

Two degradation modes cannot be accelerated by duty compression:
- calendar-driven degradation (thermal cycling, lubricant creep and outgassing, dust accumulation between operations);
- milligravity dust transport.

These need separate tests and modelling.

**AD²: 6** (several competing approaches; the path is not clear).

The competing approaches are:
- labyrinth/shroud plus EDS;
- hermetic bellows or magnetically coupled feedthroughs (no sliding seal);
- flexure and non-contact designs;
- sacrificial, swap-able wear modules.

It is not clear which works for feed locks under dusty gas pressure or for kV rotary transfer. There is an element-specific wrinkle: magnetic couplings and ferrofluid seals, the obvious vacuum options, **attract free Fe-Ni fines**.

| Element | AD² |
|---|---|
| Shrouded actuators | 4 |
| Excavation bearings | 5 |
| kV reel | 5–6 |
| Dusty-feed gas seals | 6 |
| Rotating-furnace interface | 7 |

The rotating-furnace interface needs new engineering approaches unless the whole module spins and transfer is done without a bearing, which moves the problem to the dock and transfer interface.

**Years to target:** 5–9.

## 4. Path

| # | Step | Method | Scale | Cost (USD) | Duration | Reaches |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | NEA regolith environment specification: grain size and shape, metal fraction, charging, cohesion, ejecta from excavation. Synthesise Itokawa, Ryugu and Bennu sample data and plan in-situ measurements on the scouts | Literature + analysis | Desk study + sample-data review | 0.5–2 M | 0.5–1.5 yr | Enables the TRL 4 environment-definition criterion |
| 2 | Metal-bearing NEA simulant (silicate + Fe-Ni) and a dusty thermal-vacuum facility with UV/electron charging and thermal cycling | Experiment | 1–2 m³ chamber; tonne-scale simulant | 3–10 M | 1–2 yr | Enabling infrastructure |
| 3 | Component screening of bearings, seals and connectors: MoS₂ vs PFPE; labyrinth vs bellows vs magnetic coupling; EDS-protected interfaces; kV slip-ring arcing and tracking tests in dust | Experiment | Coupon and component scale, 100s–1,000s h | 3–8 M | 1–2 yr | 4 |
| 4 | Wear and leak models (abrasive wear vs sliding distance and particle loading; seal leak vs dust ingress) correlated to steps 3 and 5 | Simulation + analysis | Model | 1–3 M | Concurrent | Supports 4–5 |
| 5 | Accelerated endurance of full-scale actuators, excavator bearings, tether reel at 1–3 kV, and the route-specific feed lock under charged simulant. Run at 100% duty to 1.5× life | Experiment | Flight-scale components, 0.7–1.9 yr continuous per article, several articles | 10–30 M | 2–3 yr | 5 |
| 6 | Milligravity dust transport and ingress. Parabolic flights and drop towers for the physics (seconds only). A scout-hosted exposure package: a small actuator and seal coupon on a touch-and-go or anchoring scout | Experiment | Seconds (ground); weeks–months (scout) | 5–20 M incremental | 2–4 yr (tied to scout schedule) | Strengthens 5; part of the relevant environment for 6 |
| 7 | Pathfinder demonstrator. Operate an excavator head + tether reel + feed lock at operational duty for at least 1 yr at an NEA. A lunar CLPS-class host is a cheaper partial analogue: right vacuum and charging, wrong gravity regime. Correlate the wear model and extrapolate to 5 yr | Experiment (flight) | Subsystem prototype | 50–200 M (T24 share of pathfinder) | 2–4 yr incl. ops | 6 (life by validated extrapolation) |

**On step 7.** A full 5-year life in the true environment cannot be demonstrated before KDP-0B. TRL 6 at KDP-0B will therefore rest on ground endurance testing plus flight correlation over at least 20% of life. The KDP-0B board should accept or reject that basis explicitly.

## 5. Risk and fallback

**Risk class: architecture-change.** If T24 misses TRL 6, the architecture can shift to the following, at a cost in spares mass, availability and makeup gas:
- swap-able wear modules;
- more robots at lower duty each;
- hermetic designs only, with no sliding seals;
- fewer rotating or pressurised interfaces, favouring the native-metal route.

The class escalates to **project-ending for 0B** if demonstrated mean time between replacement of the excavation or feed-seal elements falls below about 6–12 months. That threshold is my estimate. Below it, spares logistics on 1.5–5-year tug round trips and the resulting availability loss are likely to fail the economics gate.

For the rotating-furnace route, failure of the spin interface is effectively route-ending.

**Fallback:** Select the minimal-mechanism, native-metal route with swap-able sacrificial wear modules and hermetic (bellows or flexure) seals. If KDP-0B life evidence still fails, fall back under D-02 to "0A only, Earth supply".

## 6. Where others might disagree

1. **"Heritage puts it higher (TRL 5–6)."** One argument cites Yutu-2's more than 5 years, Opportunity's 14 years and terrestrial mining. My view is that these match on calendar time but miss on operating hours by orders of magnitude, on regolith handled by about 10⁶×, and on environment (Mars atmosphere; lunar 1/6 g vs milligravity). They also include no excavation or dusty pressure seals. I consider this the most likely upward challenge, and I reject it under the scale rule.
2. **"Milligravity is benign."** In milligravity, dust does not settle into seals and normal loads are low, so abrasion could be milder than on the Moon. The counter-argument is that cohesion, electrostatic adhesion and excavation-generated ejecta dominate, and that clean Fe-Ni grains in vacuum may adhere or gall. This is genuinely uncertain. Step 6 is designed to resolve it.
3. **Lumping vs splitting.** One could rate only the weakest element per route, making the rotating-furnace route TRL 2 / AD² 7 and the native-metal route TRL 3 / AD² 5. My single family rating of 3 (range 2–4) hides that spread. The per-element table is the operative rating.
4. **Risk class.** A reviewer focused on the economics gate may call this project-ending. A reviewer focused on design flexibility may call it cost-increase. I keep architecture-change, with the explicit escalation threshold above.
5. **Citations I could not pin down.** I am confident specific NASA KSC/GRC dust-tolerant connector, seal and RASSOR test reports exist, but I cannot cite them. If those reports contain vacuum endurance data at 10³ h or more, the excavation and connector elements might move to TRL 4. That literature check (part of step 1) should precede any upgrade.

## Gemini 3.1 Pro


### 1. Evidence

The requirement is for bearings, seals, rotary joints, and connectors to operate in hard vacuum and abrasive, electrostatically charged regolith for ≥5 years. 

Heritage systems have demonstrated subsets of these requirements, but not the combination:
- **Mars Rovers (Curiosity, Perseverance, 2012–present):** Have operated for >5–10 years in abrasive dust, utilizing labyrinth seals and specialized lubricants. However, Mars has a partial atmosphere (not hard vacuum), which significantly alters tribology and prevents the vacuum-welding and extreme outgassing seen in space.
- **Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV, 1971–1972):** Operated in hard vacuum and highly abrasive lunar dust, but only for a few days. 
- **ISS Solar Alpha Rotary Joints (SARJ, 2007–present):** Continuous operation in hard vacuum for >15 years, but without abrasive dust exposure.
- **OSIRIS-REx / Hayabusa2 (2020 / 2019):** Operated mechanisms in NEA vacuum and dust, but exposure was limited to brief sampling events, not 5 years of continuous mining duty.
- **Ground Testing (NASA KSC / GRC, ongoing):** Component-level testing of bearings, labyrinth seals, and dry-film lubricants in dusty thermal vacuum (TVAC) chambers using lunar simulants (e.g., JSC-1A, NU-LHT) for Artemis and CLPS preparations.

Ratio to required scale: Duration demonstrated in relevant vacuum/dust environment is currently on the order of weeks/months (accelerated testing) or minutes (flight), compared to the required 5 years (ratio ~0.01 to 0.1).

### 2. Current TRL

**Current TRL: 4–5**
- **Min (4):** Component and breadboard validation in a laboratory environment (dusty vacuum chambers) is well documented for lunar simulants.
- **Max (5):** Subsystem validation in a relevant environment has been partially achieved for near-term lunar applications, though not yet validated for 5-year continuous duty cycles.
- **Unmet exit criterion (TRL 6):** Documented test performance of a system or subsystem prototype (e.g., a full mining robot actuator assembly) in a relevant environment (vacuum + charged abrasive dust) demonstrating performance equivalent to a 5-year life.

### 3. Target and difficulty

**Target:** TRL 6 by KDP-0B.
**AD²: 5** (New development; similar development has not been done for this specific combination of extreme duration, vacuum, and charged dust, but the path—accelerated life testing in dusty TVAC—is clear).

### 4. Path

1. **Component Accelerated Life Testing:** Dusty TVAC testing of candidate seals, bearings, and lubricants (dry film and low-outgassing wet) using charged NEA simulants. Scale: 1:1 components. Cost: $2M–$5M. Duration: 1–2 years. Reaches TRL 5.
2. **Subsystem Prototype Demonstration:** Long-duration testing of an integrated rotary joint or wheel drive assembly in dusty TVAC, using accelerated wear profiles to simulate 5 years of operation. Scale: 1:1 subsystem. Cost: $5M–$15M. Duration: 2–3 years. Reaches TRL 6.

### 5. Risk and fallback

**Risk if fail:** Project-ending for 0B. If mechanisms seize, mining and processing operations halt, destroying the economic case.
**Fallback:** 0A only, Earth supply; or architecture change to highly redundant, short-life replaceable robotic modules (drastically increasing Phase 1 mass and cost).

### 6. Where others might disagree

Some might argue TRL is higher (TRL 6+) based on Mars rover heritage. However, the lack of an atmosphere fundamentally changes lubricant behavior and dust adhesion (vacuum welding, static charge without atmospheric dissipation), making Mars heritage insufficient for a TRL 6 rating in a hard vacuum NEA environment.

## GPT-6.1 Sol


## T24 — Dust-tolerant long-life mechanisms and seals

**Assessment: TRL 3–4; target TRL 6 at KDP-0B; AD² 6.** Long-life space mechanisms and mechanisms exposed briefly to extraterrestrial dust both have substantial heritage. Their combination—**five-year service in abrasive, charged NEA regolith, including production machinery and 1–3 kV connectors—does not have demonstrated heritage identified here.**

This is a technology-family assessment, not certification of a particular bearing, seal or connector design.

### Assessment assumptions

- **Life:** five years installed without crew servicing. Robotic replacement is permissible only if explicitly incorporated into the architecture.
- **Mining duty:** five years is approximately **43,830 elapsed hours**. At 9–25% duty, mining mechanisms accumulate approximately **3,945–10,958 operating hours**. Plant mechanisms may have substantially higher duty; that requirement remains unspecified.
- **Scale:** mechanisms serve 2–3.5 t mining robots excavating 0.5–5 t/h, processing equipment, and 1–3 kV tether interfaces. Robot mass and excavation rate are **not** bearing-load or seal-size specifications.
- **Connectors:** assume de-energized mating and demating, followed by operation at 1–3 kV. Dust-contaminated live mating would be a separate, more difficult requirement.
- **Environment:** vacuum, NEA thermal cycling at 0.9–1.3 AU, radiation, and abrasive charged particles. Dust size distribution, mineralogy, charge distribution, exposure flux and temperature limits are not yet specified.
- **Scope:** processing seals include dust containment, but a dust seal alone does not establish qualification for carbonyl chemistry, hydrogen containment or molten-metal service.

## 1. Evidence

The ratios below are **required ÷ demonstrated**. Where environments differ, a duration ratio is not an equivalence claim.

| Evidence | Demonstration and limitations | Ratio to requirement |
|---|---|---|
| **Apollo surface equipment; NASA, *Apollo 17 Mission Report*, 1973; James R. Gaier, *The Effects of Lunar Dust on EVA Systems During the Apollo Missions*, NASA/TM-2005-213610, 2005** | Flight mechanisms, equipment interfaces and protective arrangements experienced lunar vacuum and abrasive dust. Apollo documented dust-related interference, abrasion and operational difficulties. Apollo 17 provided approximately 75 hours of surface exposure—not 75 hours of continuous mechanism operation. This is direct evidence of the hazard and short-duration operation, not five-year qualification. | Elapsed-life ratio approximately **584×**. Load, particle-dose and cycle-count ratios are not established. Lunar exposure does not reproduce NEA particle transport. |
| **ISS Solar Alpha Rotary Joint; NASA STS-126 mission, 2008, and subsequent ISS operations** | Large rotary-joint operation in vacuum; inspection, cleaning and lubrication followed damage in the starboard joint. Demonstrates substantial space rotary-mechanism heritage and the importance of tribology and maintainability. It does **not** demonstrate abrasive-regolith tolerance, and crew intervention is incompatible with the assumed maintenance regime. | **n/a** for dust dose and unattended life. No suitable demonstrated load/lifetime equivalence is established here. |
| **Curiosity rover; NASA/JPL Mars Science Laboratory, 2012–2024 operations** | More than twelve years of robotic operation in a dusty planetary environment, including mobility and instrument mechanisms. Relevant to dust exclusion, protection and autonomous operation. Mars has an atmosphere and different gravity, charging and thermal conditions; this is not vacuum-regolith qualification. | Elapsed-life ratio **≤0.42**, but required/demonstrated vacuum exposure and dust-dose ratios are **n/a**. Individual mechanism operating hours differ substantially from mission elapsed time. |
| **Hayabusa2 sampling; JAXA, 2019 sampling operations and 2020 sample return** | Sampling mechanisms operated at Ryugu in NEA vacuum and microgravity, with particle contact and successful sample return. Relevant evidence for short-duration NEA mechanism operation, not repeated mining duty or seal endurance. | **n/a**: no comparable five-year wear-cycle or dust-dose demonstration. |
| **NASA Electrodynamic Dust Shield on Firefly Blue Ghost Mission 1, 2025** | NASA reported lunar-surface dust-removal demonstration. Supports an active dust-mitigation approach. It does not establish bearing/seal protection, high-voltage connector reliability, or five-year endurance. | **n/a** for protected-mechanism life and cumulative dust dose. |

**Evidence limitation:** I am confident these programmes and reports exist. I have not identified, with sufficient confidence to cite, a test report demonstrating a representative production bearing/seal/connector assembly under the combined required environment with a validated five-year life prediction. Such reports should be sought during the evidence audit; their absence from this assessment is not proof that none exist.

### Route-specific assessment

| Route | Current TRL for its T24 implementation | Principal additional burden |
|---|---:|---|
| **No-melt: beneficiation → carbonyl or H₂ route** | **3–4** | Beneficiation drives and seals share the mining dust problem. Chemical-process isolation adds pressure, leakage and material-compatibility requirements. Lunar dust heritage does not qualify carbonyl or hydrogen process seals. |
| **Rotating 0.05–0.15 g smelting furnace** | **3–4**, with the lower bound more defensible for the combined subsystem | Rotating supports, feed/discharge interfaces, thermal distortion and hot abrasive material must work together. The dust-facing feed hardware need not be at melt temperature, but any thermal isolation assumption must be demonstrated. |
| **Narrow native-metal production, rotating modules experimentally gated** | **3–4** | Cold processing reduces the thermal and chemical burden. It does not remove abrasive wear, charging, dust transport or unattended-life requirements. Avoiding dynamic process seals could materially simplify qualification. |

These are separate assessments with the same present range—not an averaging of route readiness.

## 2. Current TRL and unmet exit criterion

**Lower bound: TRL 3.** Physical operations validate critical functions: protected mechanisms can operate in dusty extraterrestrial settings; rotary mechanisms can operate in space; sampling mechanisms can contact NEA material.

**Upper bound: TRL 4, conditional on the selected component.** This is defensible where an existing component has documented laboratory performance against predictions and a documented relevant-environment definition. The programme-level heritage above does not, by itself, establish those records for every proposed mechanism.

Two distinct gaps remain:

- **From TRL 3 to 4:** a selected breadboard requires documented laboratory tests agreeing with predictions and an explicit environmental specification.
- **From TRL 4 to 5:** it requires tests in the relevant environment, with documented scaling from test loads, particle exposure, cycles and accelerated ageing to the required installation and life.

I would **not credit TRL 5** merely because an analogous component flew briefly, or TRL 9 because another bearing operated for years in a different environment.

## 3. Target and difficulty

- **0A internal target:** TRL 4–5 before selecting the pathfinder’s mechanism designs. Flight hardware also needs mission-specific qualification; a technology milestone does not replace that.
- **0B target:** **TRL 6 before KDP-0B**, for the mechanism chains whose failure would halt mining or production. No calendar date for KDP-0B is supplied.
- **Planning interval:** approximately **5–8 years from a funded start**, with overlapping development and endurance testing.
- **AD²: 6**, using the supplied project anchors. Competing approaches exist—exclusion seals, labyrinths, protected lubrication, active dust removal, replaceable cartridges and contactless interfaces—but the winning combination is not yet clear.

The main difficulty is not new physics. It is validating life under coupled particle ingress, charging, wear, thermal distortion and intermittent operation. A cold, replaceable native-metal implementation could justify **AD² 5** once requirements are fixed; the rotating hot-process implementation may remain at **6–7** until its interfaces are demonstrated.

## 4. Path to TRL 6

Costs are **rough-order-of-magnitude assessor estimates in constant 2026 USD**, not quotations. They exclude launch, the full plant and general site infrastructure. Durations overlap.

| Step | Scale and method | Cost | Duration | Exit supported |
|---|---|---:|---:|---|
| **Requirements and heritage audit** | Recover test reports; define loads, speeds, leakage, connector current, mating cycles, contamination limits and route-specific temperatures. Specify particle size, mineralogy, charge and exposure envelopes. | $0.2–0.6 million | 0.3–0.8 yr | Closes evidence gaps; **does not independently raise TRL**. |
| **Component breadboards** | Representative bearing/seal cartridges and full-voltage connector interfaces. Measure torque, wear, leakage, contact resistance and insulation performance under controlled abrasive contamination. Compare with pre-test predictions. | $1–4 million | 1–2 yr | **TRL 4** |
| **Combined relevant-environment tests** | Full-scale critical interfaces in vacuum with thermal cycling, controlled charged dust and representative loads. Address radiation-sensitive materials. Use reduced-gravity tests or validated particle-transport models anchored to such tests; do not assume Earth-gravity dust ingress is conservative. | $4–12 million | 1.5–3 yr | **TRL 5** |
| **Integrated endurance demonstration** | Representative excavation/feed mechanism, rotary process module and tether interface, tested separately where their environments differ. Demonstrate cumulative cycles and exposure; maintain parallel long-duration articles. For smelting, test the relevant 0.05–0.15 g rotating arrangement. | $10–30 million | 4–6 yr | **TRL 6**, only with documented agreement between predictions and measured subsystem performance |

**Life-test caution:** increased dust concentration, speed or temperature can change the failure mechanism. Five-year equivalence requires a validated acceleration model, not simply “five years’ dust mass” passed through a seal. Long idle periods, cold starts and connector contamination must remain in the test programme.

## 5. Risk and fallback

**Primary classification: project-ending for the specified five-year, unattended 0B architecture.** Failure of production-critical mechanisms can defeat sustained throughput. An isolated noncritical connector failure may instead create a schedule delay or cost increase.

**Fallback:** redesign around shorter-life, robotically replaceable sealed cartridges, protected cold processing and fewer exposed dynamic interfaces; qualify that replacement architecture independently. If autonomous maintenance and revised delivered cost do not pass KDP-0B, retain **0A only and Earth supply**.

A lower maintenance interval is an architecture change—not evidence that the original five-year requirement was met.

## 6. Where others might disagree

1. **TRL 4 versus 5:** a particular dust-tested bearing or seal may have relevant-environment evidence sufficient for TRL 5. I would accept that component-specific rating after reviewing its test conditions and scaling record, not extend it automatically to the whole mechanism family.
2. **Whether life is a TRL issue:** some assessors separate endurance qualification from maturity. Here, life is an essential required characteristic; an unsupported five-year extrapolation cannot satisfy relevant-environment readiness.
3. **Lunar dust as a surrogate:** lunar material may be more abrasive than some NEA material, but NEA charging, low-gravity transport and composition can change ingress. “Lunar is conservative” needs experimental support.
4. **Replaceability:** accepting frequent robotic cartridge changes can substantially reduce development difficulty, but changes availability, logistics and economics.
5. **Hot versus cold routes:** the cold native-metal route may prove substantially easier. That advantage remains a hypothesis until representative protected mechanisms are tested.

# Consolidated rating: T24, Dust-tolerant long-life mechanisms and seals

## 1. Ratings by model

| | Claude Opus 5.5 | Gemini 3.1 Pro | GPT-6.1 Sol |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Current TRL** | **2–4**. Governing rating 3. Per-element ratings run from 2 (rotating-furnace interface) to 4–5 (shrouded low-duty mobility). | **4–5** | **3–4**. All three metallurgy routes rated 3–4; for the rotating furnace, "lower bound more defensible". |
| **AD²** | **6**. Element range 4–7: furnace interface 7, dusty-feed gas seals 6, kV reel 5–6. | **5** | **6**. Could fall to 5 for the cold native-metal route once requirements are fixed; 6–7 for the rotating hot route. |
| **Target** | TRL 5 at the 0A mid-term review; TRL 6 at KDP-0B (KDP-0B assumed to fall around 2032–34). | TRL 6 at KDP-0B | TRL 4–5 during 0A, before pathfinder mechanism selection; TRL 6 before KDP-0B (no date given). |
| **Risk if fail** | **Architecture-change.** Escalates to project-ending if the mean time between replacement (MTBR) of excavation or feed-seal elements falls below about 6–12 months (Claude's own estimate). Failure of the spin interface ends the rotating-furnace route. | **Project-ending** | **Project-ending** for the specified 5-year unattended architecture. An isolated noncritical connector failure would only cause schedule delay or cost increase. |
| **Years to target** | 5–9 | 2–4 | 5–8 |
| **Self-stated confidence** | medium | high | medium |
| **Path cost (sum of stated step ranges)** | about $73M–$273M, including a flight pathfinder | about $7M–$20M | about $15M–$47M |

## 2. Where the models agree

- **Target and need.** TRL 6 is required before KDP-0B. The phase need is 0B.
- **The combination is not demonstrated.** All three say no heritage covers the combination of hard vacuum, charged abrasive regolith and 5-year life.
- **Mars heritage does not transfer.** All three discount it because of the atmosphere, gravity and dust character.
  - Claude cites Opportunity.
  - Gemini cites Curiosity and Perseverance.
  - GPT cites Curiosity.
  - All three anticipate an upward challenge based on Mars heritage and reject it.
- **Apollo shows the hazard.** Apollo is treated as short-duration evidence of the dust hazard, not as qualification.
- **ISS SARJ shows clean-vacuum rotary heritage only.** It is evidence for rotary mechanisms in vacuum without dust.
- **Hayabusa2 shows only brief NEA contact.** All three treat it as evidence of short-duration mechanism contact with NEA material, not endurance.
- **Operating-hour requirement.** Claude (about 4,000–11,000 h) and GPT (3,945–10,958 h) independently derive the same figure for mining mechanisms at 9–25% duty. Gemini does not compute it.
- **Fallback.** All three include short-life, robotically swappable modules or cartridges, and ultimately "0A only, Earth supply".
- **RQ register.** None assigns related research-question IDs.

## 3. Where they diverge and why

### 3.1 Current TRL: 4–5 (Gemini) vs 3–4 (GPT) vs 2–4 (Claude)

The models rely on different evidence.

**Gemini** bases TRL 4 on NASA KSC/GRC component-level dusty thermal-vacuum (TVAC) testing with lunar simulants (JSC-1A, NU-LHT). Its YAML marks this evidence confident, but it cites no specific report; the source field reads "~2010s-2020s". Gemini's upper bound of 5 rests on subsystem validation "partially achieved for near-term lunar applications", again with no citation.

**Claude** refers to the same body of work (KSC/GRC connector and seal tests, RASSOR) but marks it **unsure** and says it cannot cite specific endurance reports. Claude also holds TRL 4 unmet on a second ground: there is no documented relevant-environment definition. In particular, no validated metal-bearing NEA simulant exists, and no charging or excavation-dust data exist. Claude states that if KSC/GRC reports show vacuum endurance of 10³ h or more, the excavation and connector elements might move to TRL 4.

**GPT** says it has not identified such a report with enough confidence to cite. It explicitly notes that absence from its assessment is not proof that none exist. It allows TRL 4 only where a specific component has a documented lab-vs-prediction record and an environment definition.

The models also disagree on simulant relevance:
- Gemini accepts lunar simulants.
- GPT says "lunar is conservative" needs experimental support.
- Claude says no NEA simulant exists to define the environment.

**What would settle it:**
- Retrieve and review the actual KSC/GRC dust-tolerant mechanism, seal and connector test reports. The review should record vacuum level, simulant, charging, load, duration and whether results were compared against predictions.
- Produce a documented NEA relevant-environment specification, as in Claude's path step 1 and GPT's path step 1.
- Run a comparative lunar-vs-NEA simulant test to answer whether lunar dust is a conservative surrogate.

### 3.2 Granularity, and the ratings of the furnace interface and kV joint

| Element | Claude | GPT | Gemini |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rotating-furnace spin interface | TRL 2. Uses the 2007 SARJ race damage and the Galileo HGA as negative evidence, and states there is no critical-function test. | TRL 3–4 for the route; lower bound more defensible. | Not separately addressed. |
| 1–3 kV rotary joint | TRL 2–3. Comsat SADA slip rings are only at about 100 V class in clean vacuum, and Claude raises arcing and Paschen-regime concerns. | Plans full-voltage connector tests. Assumes de-energised mating, and says live mating in dust would be a separate, harder requirement. | Not addressed. |
| Dusty-feed process seals for carbonyl or H₂ routes | TRL 2–3. The 10–100+ bar pressure figure is Claude's own assumption from terrestrial practice. | Says lunar heritage does not qualify these seals. | Not addressed. |

The two models also frame SARJ differently:
- Claude treats it as a lubrication-breakdown failure.
- GPT treats it as heritage that shows the importance of maintainability, with crew intervention that would be incompatible with an unattended site.
- Gemini cites it as more than 15 years of continuous operation and does not mention the damage.

**What would settle it:**
- Critical-function tests of a spin/despin interface and of a 1–3 kV rotary joint, including arcing and tracking, in dusty vacuum.
- A route-specific dusty-feed lock leak test at operating gas pressure.

### 3.3 AD²: 5 vs 6

- **Gemini** treats the path as clear: accelerated life testing in dusty TVAC.
- **Claude and GPT** cite several competing approaches with no clear winner: labyrinth or shroud plus electrodynamic dust shield (EDS), bellows or magnetic coupling, non-contact designs, and replaceable cartridges.
- **Claude only** adds that magnetic couplings and ferrofluid seals would attract free Fe-Ni fines.

**What would settle it:** component screening results comparing the competing seal approaches in metal-bearing simulant (Claude step 3, GPT breadboard step).

### 3.4 Risk class: architecture-change (Claude) vs project-ending (Gemini, GPT)

The disagreement turns on whether a fallback to swappable modules stays within the project.
- **Claude** treats it as an architecture change and gives an MTBR escalation threshold.
- **GPT** states that a lower maintenance interval "is an architecture change — not evidence that the original five-year requirement was met." GPT nevertheless classes failure as project-ending for the specified architecture.
- **Gemini** argues that seizure halts operations and destroys the economic case.

**What would settle it:** a sensitivity analysis of delivered $/kg and availability against mechanism MTBR and spares logistics. Claude's 6–12 month threshold is an unvalidated estimate and could be tested by this analysis. The final classification remains a board judgement.

### 3.5 Years to target: 2–4 vs 5–9 / 5–8

The difference comes from path scope and from assumptions about life testing.

**Gemini's path has two ground steps.** It assumes accelerated wear profiles can simulate 5 years within 2–3 years.

**Claude's path is broader:**
- It adds environment specification, a simulant and facility build, milligravity tests, and a flight pathfinder with at least 1 year of operations at an NEA.
- Its arithmetic gives 0.7–1.9 years of continuous testing per article at 100% duty and a 1.5× life factor.
- It states that calendar-driven degradation and milligravity transport cannot be accelerated by duty compression.

**GPT's path is ground-based** but allows 4–6 years for integrated endurance with parallel long-duration articles. GPT cautions that raising dust concentration, speed or temperature can change the failure mechanism, so a validated acceleration model is needed.

**What would settle it:**
- A validated acceleration model showing failure-mode equivalence between accelerated and nominal conditions. Claude step 4 and GPT's life-test caution both call for this.
- A board decision on whether TRL 6 requires flight correlation. Claude asks the KDP-0B board to accept or reject explicitly a basis of ground testing plus flight correlation over at least 20% of life.

### 3.6 Milligravity dust behaviour

- **Claude** calls it genuinely uncertain whether milligravity makes abrasion milder or worse, citing cohesion, electrostatics, ejecta and possible Fe-Ni galling.
- **GPT** says Earth-gravity ingress must not be assumed conservative.
- **Gemini** is silent.

**What would settle it:** reduced-gravity ingress tests plus an exposure package hosted on a scout (Claude step 6), or particle-transport models anchored to reduced-gravity tests (GPT).

## 4. Evidence cited

### Cited by more than one model

| Evidence | Models | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Gaier, NASA/TM-2005-213610 (2005), Apollo dust effects | Claude, GPT | Both confident. Gemini cites the Apollo LRV with no reference. |
| ISS SARJ | All three | Framing differs; see 3.2. Claude dates the damage to 2007; GPT cites the STS-126 cleaning and lubrication (2008). |
| Hayabusa2 at Ryugu (2019–20) | All three | Short-duration evidence only. |
| Electrodynamic Dust Shield on Firefly Blue Ghost M1 (2025) | Claude, GPT | GPT is confident. **Claude is internally inconsistent**: its text says "fairly confident" but its YAML marks it `confident: false`. Covers surfaces only, not sliding seals. |
| Curiosity (2012–) | Gemini, GPT | Environment mismatch acknowledged by both. |
| NASA KSC/GRC dusty-vacuum component tests | Claude (unsure), Gemini (confident, no specific report) | **Pivotal for the TRL divergence. No model provides a citable report.** GPT does not cite it. |

### Cited by one model only

**Claude only:**
- Lunokhod 1 and 2. Distances are approximate. The end of Lunokhod 2 is attributed to dust contamination of the radiator.
- Yutu-2. Claude is **unsure** of the traverse figure.
- MER Opportunity. Claude is **unsure** of the Spirit wheel-failure attribution.
- Hayabusa (Itokawa).
- OSIRIS-REx TAGSAM flap jammed open by particles, given as negative evidence. Gemini mentions OSIRIS-REx only generically.
- Galileo HGA.
- Comsat SADA and ESTL practice. No single programme is cited.
- Tsuchiyama et al., *Science* (2011), on Itokawa grains.
- RASSOR. Claude is **unsure** of this one.
- Terrestrial lock hoppers.

**GPT only:**
- NASA *Apollo 17 Mission Report* (1973), with about 75 h of surface exposure and a ratio of about 584× in elapsed life.

**Gemini only:**
- Perseverance.
- Named lunar simulants (JSC-1A, NU-LHT) used in the KSC/GRC tests, with no report cited.

### Ratio convention

The brief asks for ratios as required ÷ demonstrated.
- Claude and GPT use required ÷ demonstrated (for example, GPT's 584× for Apollo 17).
- Gemini reports demonstrated ÷ required ("~0.01 to 0.1"; YAML "0.001", "0.1"). Its ratios should be inverted before comparison.
- GPT's Curiosity ratio of "≤0.42" is also below 1 because Curiosity's demonstrated life exceeds the requirement. GPT marks this as elapsed life only.

## 5. Consolidated path

This is the union of the three paths with attribution. Where costs differ, all stated ranges are shown and none is chosen.

| # | Step | Proposed by | Cost (USD) | Duration | Reaches |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Requirements and heritage audit.** Recover the KSC/GRC test reports; define loads, speeds, leak limits, kV and connector duty, and mate cycles. This should precede any TRL upgrade. | GPT; Claude (within its step 1, and section 6 item 5) | GPT 0.2–0.6M | 0.3–0.8 yr | Resolves the 3.1 dispute; no TRL increase on its own |
| 2 | **NEA relevant-environment specification**: grain properties, metal fraction, charging, ejecta. Draws on Itokawa, Ryugu and Bennu sample data and on scout measurements. | Claude; GPT (within its audit) | Claude 0.5–2M | 0.5–1.5 yr | Required for the TRL 4 environment criterion (Claude) |
| 3 | **Metal-bearing NEA simulant and a dusty TVAC facility** with charging and thermal cycling. | Claude. Gemini assumes "charged NEA simulants" without a development step. | 3–10M | 1–2 yr | Enabling |
| 4 | **Component screening and breadboards**: bearings, seals, lubricants, competing seal concepts, kV slip-ring arcing tests. | All three | Claude 3–8M; GPT 1–4M; Gemini 2–5M | 1–2 yr | TRL 4 (Claude, GPT); TRL 5 (Gemini) |
| 5 | **Wear, leak and acceleration models** correlated to tests. | Claude; GPT (validated acceleration model) | Claude 1–3M | concurrent | Supports 4–5 |
| 6 | **Relevant-environment and full-scale component endurance** to 1.5× life (Claude), or combined-environment tests (GPT). | Claude, GPT | Claude 10–30M; GPT 4–12M | 1.5–3 yr | TRL 5 |
| 7 | **Milligravity dust transport**: parabolic and drop-tower tests, plus a scout-hosted exposure package (Claude) or reduced-gravity-anchored models (GPT). | Claude, GPT | Claude 5–20M | 2–4 yr, tied to the scout schedule | Strengthens TRL 5 |
| 8 | **Integrated subsystem demonstration.** The models propose different forms. | All three | Claude 50–200M (flight); GPT 10–30M; Gemini 5–15M | Claude 2–4 yr; GPT 4–6 yr; Gemini 2–3 yr | TRL 6 |

The three forms of step 8 are:
- **Claude:** a flight pathfinder operating an excavator head, tether reel and feed lock for at least 1 year at an NEA. A lunar CLPS-class host is offered as a partial analogue.
- **GPT:** ground integrated endurance, testing mining, process-module and tether hardware separately, including a rotating arrangement at 0.05–0.15 g for the smelting route.
- **Gemini:** ground dusty-TVAC subsystem testing with accelerated wear.

**Fallbacks proposed:**
- All three propose swappable short-life modules or cartridges, then "0A only, Earth supply".
- Claude and GPT add a minimal-mechanism or cold native-metal route.
- Claude adds hermetic (bellows or flexure) seals.

## 6. Open items for the board

The panel's conclusions currently turn on these items. They are not resolved here.

1. **KSC/GRC reports.** Do they contain dusty-vacuum endurance data on representative components? This item controls whether the current rating is 3 or 4–5.
2. **Lunar simulant as surrogate.** Is lunar simulant an acceptable surrogate for the NEA relevant environment, or is a metal-bearing NEA simulant required?
